titleText.es: —¿Te recojo a las ocho? —A las nueve. Tengo que volver a minar el camino de entrada.
titleText.en: 'Pick you up at eight?' 'Nine.  I've got to re-mine the driveway.'
titleText.noteEn: The official title text continues the pair's mutual booby-trapping joke: the pickup time must allow the driveway to be mined again. The Spanish archive uses the same joke with volver a minar.

regions.labelEs: ME RINDO. TÚ GANAS. TENGO QUE SABER QUIÉN ERES.

applications.explanationEn: Me is the matching short marker that makes rindo the give-up form of rendirse.
Tengo matches the speaker, que completes the obligation pattern, and saber stays in its unchanged -er dictionary form.
Quién introduces the unknown identity inside the larger saber statement, so it keeps its written accent; eres supplies the embedded action.

regions.labelEs: NOS ENTENDEMOS EL UNO AL OTRO. NO PUEDO DEJAR PASAR ESO...

applications.explanationEn: Nos supplies the mutual marker, so entendemos describes an understanding shared between the people involved.
El uno identifies one member of the mixed pair, and al otro combines a with el before the other member.
Puedo matches the speaker, and dejar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form as the possible action.
After dejar, pasar describes allowing the referenced situation to go by rather than holding on to it.
Ha is the helper for one thing, and sido is ser's completed-action form.
Minas names the devices, and the descriptive word remotas follows that noun in the neutral order.
Remotas ends in -as to match the feminine plural noun minas.

regions.labelEs: AH, ESO. LAS MOVÍ A TU GARAJE ANTES DE LLAMAR A LA PUERTA.

applications.explanationEn: Las replaces the already identified feminine plural items and appears directly before the changed verb moví.
The -í ending presents the move as one bounded, completed past action by the speaker.
Antes de introduces the later event, and llamar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Llamar supplies the action, and the fixed words a la puerta give it the door-knocking sense.
Va matches the singular subject, a links the pieces, and ser stays in its unchanged -er dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: TODAVÍA HAY TIEMPO PARA IRTE Y BUSCAR UNA CHICA NO LOCA.

applications.exampleEs: HAY TIEMPO PARA IRTE Y BUSCAR
applications.explanationEn: Hay tiempo para introduces available time, and irte and buscar are the two coordinated actions kept in their dictionary forms.
Te is attached directly to the unchanged verb ir, making the one-word form irte.
Chica names the person, while the descriptive word loca follows it; no negates that description without changing the order.
Loca ends in -a to match the feminine singular noun chica; no does not change.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.answerEn: I give up; I surrender (with me)
cards.noteEn: Rindo is a present form of rendir. With the matching short marker me, it forms rendirse, the usual verb for giving up or surrendering.

example.es: Me rindo después de tres intentos.
example.en: I give up after three attempts.

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.answerEn: each other; marks a shared action involving “us”
cards.noteEn: With a plural verb, nos can show that the speakers do the action to or with each other. Context distinguishes this reciprocal use from nos meaning simply “us.”
Entendemos is the present form of entender for “we.” With reciprocal nos, it describes understanding shared between the people in that “we.” Without nos, it can simply mean “we understand.”

cards.questionEn: How do you make it explicit that two people do something to each other?
cards.answerEn: Use el uno al otro for two masculine people or a mixed pair; change the endings when the people are feminine.
cards.noteEn: The expression literally pairs “the one” with “the other.” Use la una a la otra for two feminine people. It often appears with nos, se, or another small object word when the verb needs one.

example.es: Nos ayudamos el uno al otro.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: to pass; to slip away (after dejar)
cards.noteEn: After dejar, pasar can describe allowing an opportunity, moment, or situation to go by instead of acting on it.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Sido is the completed-action form of ser. It follows a form of haber: ha sido means “has been,” and haber sido means “to have been.”

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Remotas normally means far away. With a device, it can describe operation or activation from a distance. Its -as ending matches a feminine plural noun.
Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.
Before a changed verb, las can replace a feminine plural noun that is already understood. Spanish puts this short object word before the verb: las guardé means “I stored them.”

example.es: Compré las llaves y las guardé.
example.en: I bought the keys and stored them.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
The written accent on í marks this completed past action by the speaker.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

cards.promptEs: antes de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one action happens before another action by the same person?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de, then keep the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as salir, comer, or escribir. Use antes de directly before that form when no new subject is named. If the later action has its own stated subject, Spanish normally uses antes de que and a different verb form.

example.es: Apaga la luz antes de salir.
example.en: Turn off the light before leaving.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links antes to the following action
cards.noteEn: Keep de after antes when the next action stays in its unchanged dictionary form: antes de salir. English expresses the sequence with 'before' and does not translate de separately.

example.es: Lávate las manos antes de comer.

cards.noteEn: Llamar often means “to call.” In the fixed expression llamar a la puerta, it means to knock on a door.

example.es: Voy a llamar a la puerta.
example.en: I am going to knock on the door.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone knocks on a door?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of llamar followed by a la puerta.
cards.noteEn: Llamar usually means “to call,” but llamar a la puerta is the conventional expression for knocking on a door. Only llamar changes for the person and time; a la puerta stays unchanged unless a different door is named.

cards.answerEn: on; fixed link in llamar a la puerta
cards.noteEn: This a belongs to the conventional expression llamar a la puerta, “to knock on the door.” It is not marking movement toward a destination.
This French borrowing is used as a short reaction that admits the other person's clever reply or successful counterpoint.

cards.answerEn: is going to (before a future action)
cards.noteEn: Va normally means ‘goes.’ Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what one person or thing is going to do.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)

cards.noteEn: The opposite is fácil, ‘easy.’ Difícil keeps its written accent in the singular.

cards.promptEs: hay tiempo para + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that there is time available to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use hay tiempo para, then put the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Hay says that something exists and does not change for one thing or several. Tiempo names the available time, and para introduces its use. The following action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Other times can use había tiempo or habrá tiempo.
After tiempo, para introduces the action for which time is available. The action verb then stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Ir is the unchanged dictionary form “to go.” Attaching te makes irte, the form of irse used when one familiar person leaves or goes away.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Chica can mean a girl or young woman. Mi chica often means “my girlfriend,” but context can also use it loosely for the woman who would be right for someone.

example.en: He met a friendly young woman.

cards.noteEn: Loca is the feminine singular form of loco. Applied to an adventure, idea, or entertainment, it can describe something wildly excessive or unrestrained rather than a medical condition.
Ni can add another rejected item after a negative, or begin a short emphatic rejection. It commonly has the force of “not even.”
